board_exclusion_records.alternative_reading: The prompt lists no state income tax withheld or paid during 2026. The reference fills the state income tax part of the federal state and local tax deduction (26 U.S.C. 164(a)(3), (b)(5)) with policyengine-us's formula estimate of Virginia income tax withheld: Virginia's rate schedule applied to the person's whole federal AGI (including $19,828.80 of taxable Social Security, which Virginia exempts) less Virginia's single standard deduction (va_withheld_income_tax), $5,367.30. The same engine computes the household's Virginia income tax before refundable credits as $3,514.15. Read as the household paying its 2026 Virginia income tax during the year, the deduction takes that liability and the output is the alternative value. The prompt's rule that unlisted numeric inputs are 0 gives a third reading, no state income tax paid, under which SALT takes the general sales tax (the note gives that value).
board_exclusion_records.unlisted_input: state income tax withheld or paid during 2026, which the federal state and local tax deduction takes as its state income tax part; policyengine-us fills it with state_withheld_income_tax, a formula estimate on federal AGI that the household data never set; also Medicare enrollment and a Medicare Part B premium paid during 2026, which the medical expense deductions count; policyengine-us treats every Medicare-eligible person as enrolled (takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true, so medicare_enrolled follows is_medicare_eligible) and adds the modeled premium (medicare_part_b_premium) to medical expenses, and the household data never set either
board_exclusion_records.note: Found 2026-10-05 by sweeping every reference with the state income tax in SALT read three ways (reference_audit/2026-10-05/scripts/sweep_salt_withholding.py, on policyengine-us 2.15.17 with latest_final; its baseline reproduces all 1,928 scored references, and an independent re-implementation agreed on all 1,984 outputs). SALT is $9,431.59 in the reference and $7,578.44 under the alternative; the household itemizes under both, and the $40,400 cap binds under neither. Under the zero reading SALT takes the general sales tax, $692.40, and the output is $11,758.09; that sales tax includes the engine's local component of $115.40 (20% of the state table amount, an estimate for an unlisted locality), and without it the output is $11,783.48. The reference's medical deduction also includes a modeled Medicare Part B premium of $2,434.80, which the prompt does not list. Without it the output is $11,265.27 under the withholding estimate and $11,642.16 under the liability, and with no withholding, local sales tax or Part B premium it is $11,969.80 (the household then takes the standard deduction).

board_exclusion_records.alternative_reading: The prompt lists no Medicare enrollment and no Medicare Part B premium, and its rules say to treat any unlisted numeric input as 0 and not to infer unlisted expenses or health coverage. The reference counts a modeled Part B premium as a medical expense: policyengine-us treats the head (age 69, so Medicare-eligible) as enrolled because takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true, and medical_expense_health_insurance_premiums adds medicare_part_b_premium, the 2026 standard premium of $202.90 a month, $2,434.80, to the listed $10,000 of other medical expenses. The household itemizes, so the federal medical expense deduction (26 U.S.C. 213(a): expenses above 7.5% of AGI) counts it, and Virginia's itemized deductions, which start from the federal itemized deductions (va_itemized_deductions), carry it too. The prompt also says to assume program take-up when required, and a reader who takes a 69-year-old with Social Security retirement income to be enrolled in Part B and paying the standard premium gets the frozen value. But the benchmark sets take-up only for the programs its household data list (Medicaid, SSI, the ACA credit, the DC property tax credit, the EITC, SNAP and tax filing; policybench.scenarios.DEFAULT_TAKEUP_INPUTS), and Medicare is not among them; the Medicare request asks only whether the head is eligible; and the more specific rules against inferring unlisted expenses or health coverage point the other way. Read with no Part B premium paid, the deduction falls by $2,434.80 and the output is the alternative value.
board_exclusion_records.unlisted_input: Medicare enrollment and a Medicare Part B premium paid during 2026, which the medical expense deductions count; policyengine-us treats every Medicare-eligible person as enrolled (takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true, so medicare_enrolled follows is_medicare_eligible) and adds the modeled premium (medicare_part_b_premium) to medical expenses, and the household data never set either
board_exclusion_records.note: Found 2026-10-05 by sweeping every reference with each person's Medicare Part B premium at 0, and again with Medicare enrollment off (reference_audit/2026-10-05-medicare-part-b/scripts/sweep_part_b.py, on policyengine-us 2.15.17 with latest_final; its baseline reproduces all 1,928 scored references). Of 39 Medicare-eligible people in 33 households, the engine charges the premium in 30 (Medicare Savings Program coverage pays it for the 4 eligible people in the other 3); only this household's two tax outputs move, under either reading. The federal medical expense deduction is $4,441.86 in the reference ($12,434.80 of expenses less 7.5% of $106,572.56 AGI) and $2,007.06 without the premium; the household itemizes under both. The output also depends on the state income tax in the federal SALT deduction, which PolicyEngine/policybench#191 proposes to treat as an unlisted input (decision d963), through the federal itemization election, which Virginia follows (va_deductions reads tax_unit_itemizes). Without the premium the output is $3,654.15 under both the withholding estimate and the liability; with no state income tax paid it is $4,127.67, with or without the local sales tax estimate, because the household then takes the federal and Virginia standard deductions. With the premium it is $3,514.15 under all four readings. The premium is the standard premium: the engine reads the income-related adjustment from MAGI two years earlier, which no household sets, and at this household's 2026 MAGI ($106,572.56) none would apply. GPT-6 Astra ($3,654.16) and GPT-6.1 Sol ($3,654.66) answered within $1 of the alternative value, and no model within $1 of the frozen value.
